name: Seine (the Seine; English: Seine River)
official_name: la Seine (French; pronounced /sɛn/). The river is officially registered in the French national water reference system (Sandre - Service d'administration nationale de donnees et referentiels sur l'eau, run by the French biodiversity office OFB for Eau France / Ministry of Ecological Transition) as river code '----0010' under the name 'La Seine', status 'Validé'. It is a 'fleuve' (a river discharging into the sea). No French statute confers a special 'official designation' on the river as such: legally it is a domanial public watercourse of the State (Code general de la propriete des personnes publiques, art. L.2111-9) and a navigable waterway, and it is named in public law through the departments that take their name from it (Seine, Seine-et-Marne, Seine-Maritime, and the former Seine-et-Oise).
entity_type: River (French 'fleuve') - a natural, heavily engineered and canalised watercourse flowing entirely within metropolitan France to the English Channel. Status class: second longest river wholly inside France (after the Loire) and the shortest of France's five great rivers; a 7th-order stream (Strahler number 7 in the Sandre reference); a domanial, navigable waterway of national interest ('reseau magistral' / 'voies navigables a grand gabarit'); a European inland waterway of international importance (E 80, 'Seine') under the UNECE AGN agreement; and the main watercourse of the Seine-Normandie river-basin district set up for the EU Water Framework Directive and Flood Directive.
country: France - the whole course of the Seine lies in metropolitan France, crossing four regions from upstream to downstream: Bourgogne-Franche-Comte, Grand Est, Ile-de-France and Normandie. The only point where the hydrographic basin touches another state is the very head of the Oise (about 40 km2 in Hainaut, Wallonia, Belgium); the Seine itself is entirely French. The capital city it runs through, Paris, is the capital of France.
administrative_status: River classification / legal-administrative status. (1) Domain: the Seine is part of the public river domain of the State ('domaine public fluvial de l'Etat', CG3P art. L.2111-9), i.e. a domanial watercourse whose inviolability is protected by 'contraventions de grande voirie'; a legal study for the City of Paris (GRIDAUH, 2023) notes that the Seine is 'essentiellement' in the State domain, the notable exception being its source, owned by the City of Paris since the 1860s, and that the water itself belongs to nobody until abstracted. (2) Navigation: a large-dimension ('grand gabarit') route on the non-transferable 'reseau magistral' of waterways of national interest listed by decree n° 2005-992 of 16 August 2005; Voies navigables de France (VNF) is responsible for navigation, the channel and the river domain up to the Pont Boieldieu at Rouen (its Service de navigation sur la Seine covers the river upstream of Amfreville-sous-les-Monts), while HAROPA PORT manages the maritime reach and the Paris ports/quays and the City of Paris manages the Paris canals. Gauge classes: pushed convoys up to 5,000 t downstream of Paris, 3,000 t upstream, and ocean vessels up to 280 m / 150,000 dwt on the 120 km maritime reach Rouen-Le Havre (which VNF classifies with a maximum section gauge of 27,000 t). (3) Water policy: the Seine watershed is the core of one of France's six river-basin districts (Seine-Normandie, code F), with a distinct WFD water-body district for 'La Seine de sa source au confluent de l'Oise (exclu)' and for the Seine downstream of the Oise. (4) Hydrological class: regime 'pluvial oceanique', tidal influence up to Rouen (with the mascaret tidal bore).
is_capital_of_france: No - in the strict sense the Seine is not a capital, because it is a river and not a commune or territorial collectivity; it cannot hold capital status. In the sense intended by the research question the answer is affirmative: the Seine is the river that runs through Paris, the capital of France, splitting the capital into its Right Bank (north) and Left Bank (south) along the 13 km it flows within the city limits (Ville de Paris), and it is the geographic backbone of France's seat of government.
capital_status_details: City-side point (this field concerns Paris, not the river): capital status in France is not fixed by any constitution or organic text. The Constitution of 4 October 1958 - like every French constitution since 1791 - never names a capital; Article 2 lists the Republic's symbols (language, flag, anthem, motto) but is silent on the capital, which legal scholars describe as an 'impense constitutionnel' (Delledonne, Perspectives on Federalism, 2024). Status therefore rests on convention plus ordinary legislation: Article 1 of ordinance n° 58-1100 of 17 November 1958 on the functioning of parliamentary assemblies (in force) states 'L'Assemblee nationale et le Senat siegent a Paris', with a power to transfer the seat of public authorities to another town when circumstances require; the administrative-terminology decree (arrete) of 4 November 1993 on names of States and capitals lists Paris as the 'capitale ou siege du gouvernement' of France (replacing the 1985 arrete). The Council of Europe's Congress study 'Status of capital cities' (CPL(14)4REP, 2007) classifies Paris with Nicosia, Copenhagen, Helsinki, Lisbon and London as a conventional capital whose status is 'enshrined neither by the fundamental law nor by any other statutory regulation'. Seine-side fact: the closest thing to a legal definition of the capital operates directly on the Seine, because the two assemblies located in Paris by the 1958 ordinance sit on the river's banks - the Palais-Bourbon (National Assembly) fronts the Left Bank quay and the Palais du Luxembourg (Senate) lies about a kilometre from it - so the seat of Parliament is legally tied to a city on the Seine, and the classic image of the 1910 flood is deputies reaching the Assemblee nationale by boat.
river_running_through: The Seine. Flow path through and beyond the capital, confirmed upstream to downstream: the river rises at Source-Seine (Cote-d'Or) on the Langres Plateau, runs on a general south-east to north-west axis across the Paris Basin through Troyes, reaches the confluence with the Yonne at Montereau-Fault-Yonne, enters Ile-de-France, joins its largest right-bank affluent the Marne at Charenton-le-Pont / Alfortville / Ivry-sur-Seine, enters the city of Paris immediately below that confluence between the 12th and 13th arrondissements, flows west/north-west 13 km intra-muros, leaves towards Boulogne-Billancourt / Suresnes, passes Conflans-Sainte-Honorine (Oise confluence), Mantes-la-Jolie, Vernon, Les Andelys, Rouen, and discharges into the English Channel between Le Havre and Honfleur. Navigation engineers define the urban reach as the 'bief de Paris': 24.990 km of pooled water between the Port-a-l'Anglais dam on the Seine (and Saint-Maurice on the Marne) upstream and the Suresnes dam downstream, with a normal pool of 26.72 m NGF-IGN69 and about 3 m of guaranteed navigable depth (VNF).
relationship_between_paris_and_seine: Entry and exit. The Seine enters Paris at the city's south-eastern (upstream) limit, just downstream of the Seine-Marne confluence, between the 12th arrondissement on the right bank (Bercy) and the 13th on the left bank (Massena / Paris-Rive-Gauche, fronting Ivry-sur-Seine), and leaves it at the western (downstream) limit between the 16th arrondissement on the right bank (Passy/Auteuil and the Bois de Boulogne, fronting Suresnes and Saint-Cloud) and the 15th on the left bank (fronting Boulogne-Billancourt and Issy-les-Moulineaux); the downstream Paris limit lies between the Suresnes and aval ring-road crossings. Banks and arrondissements. Because the river flows towards the north-west it divides the commune into the 'rive droite' (north) and 'rive gauche' (south); 10 of the 20 arrondissements have river frontage - right bank 1st, 4th, 8th, 12th, 16th; left bank 5th, 6th, 7th, 13th, 15th (the 2nd, 3rd, 9th, 10th, 11th, 14th, 17th, 18th, 19th and 20th are on one bank or the other but do not touch the water). The Sandre river file counts 9 arrondissements crossed by the watercourse. Islands. Two natural islands: the Ile de la Cite (1st and 4th, 29 ha, the Lutetian/medieval core, enlarged around 1600 when the islets a la Gourdaine, aux Juifs et des Vaches were attached during the building of the Pont Neuf) and the Ile Saint-Louis (4th, 11 ha, created by the 1614 infilling of the channel between the Ile Notre-Dame and the Ile aux Vaches); one artificial island, the Ile aux Cygnes (15th, a 910 x 40 m embankment raised in 1825 for the Pont de Grenelle). Historic islands absorbed by the banks include Louviers (joined to the right bank in 1843) and Maquerelle/ile des Cygnes (joined to the left bank under the First Empire), now the port de la Bourdonnais and quai Branly. Bridges. 37 crossings within Paris, 4 of them pedestrian-only footbridges; the 37th was the Passerelle Simone-de-Beauvoir (2006), linking the Bibliotheque Francois-Mitterrand (13th) to the parc de Bercy (12th). About 257 bridges span the Seine and its arms along the whole river. Channel geometry in the city. 13 km long, from 30 m wide at the quai de Montebello (5th) to 200 m at the Pont de Grenelle (15th), 3.40-5.70 m deep, normal water height 1-2 m at the Austerlitz gauge, average flow about 310 m3/s (PIREN-Seine; the Vigicrues Austerlitz record F700000103 gives an annual mean of 316 m3/s for 2006-2026 over a 43,800 km2 catchment) - the City itself quotes 330 m3/s. After 1910 the quays were raised and protected to the 1910 level (8.60 m), several bridges were rebuilt higher and the bed was deepened at the downstream exit of Paris to pass flood flows. Quays, ports and canals. The quais are still the capital's working port estate: HAROPA PORT manages the Paris ports and quays except the 'Port des Champs-Elysees' length between the passerelle Leopold-Sedhar-Senghor and the Pont des Invalides, which VNF keeps; the Paris canals (Ourcq, Saint-Denis, Saint-Martin - about 130 km of canals in the region, decreed under Napoleon I, fed by the Ourcq as both aqueduct and waterway) meet the Seine at the bassin de la Villette, the canal Saint-Martin and the port de l'Arsenal, and let boats bypass the city. The river is also one of the principal ecological corridors of the Ile-de-France regional ecological coherence scheme (SRCE). Measurement and symbolism. The official gauge is the 'echelle d'Austerlitz' (its zero fixed at 25.92 m NGF-IGN69), monitored by DRIEAT's 'Seine Moyenne Yonne Loing' flood-forecast service and relayed daily to the Prefecture of Police and the City's monitoring centre from 2.50 m; Parisians read the river unofficially from the Zouave of the Pont de l'Alma. The Paris coat of arms (a ship under way) descends from the medieval Guild of the Merchants of the Water, the city's point zero is on the parvis of Notre-Dame on the Ile de la Cite, and the RATP logo is the outline of Paris with the Seine through it. Today the river also gives the capital three supervised public swimming sites (Bras Marie at the Ile Saint-Louis, Bras de Grenelle, Bercy), the 'Paris Plages' programme, 8-9 million excursion-boat passengers a year, urban river freight and Olympic open-water sport (2024).
location_coordinates: Source: 47 deg 29' 10" N, 4 deg 43' 01" E (Source-Seine, Cote-d'Or, about 30 km north-west of Dijon). Mouth: 49 deg 26' 02" N, 0 deg 12' 24" E (Bay of the Seine, between Le Havre and Honfleur). In Paris the river runs roughly 48 deg 51' N, 2 deg 21' E (Notre-Dame) to 48 deg 52' N, 2 deg 17' E (Pont de Grenelle) - the City of Paris centre is 48 deg 51' 24" N, 2 deg 21' 07" E. Position in the national territory: the centre of northern France, draining the Paris Basin south-east to north-west; Rouen lies 120 km from the sea, and Paris 72 km beyond the Oise confluence.
physical_setting: Relief and basin: the Seine drains the Paris Basin, France's great sedimentary lowland (chalk, limestone, marl and clay over a gently folded dome), which gives it a very low gradient - from 446 m at the source to sea level in about 775 km - and a wide, sinuous valley: downstream of Paris more than a dozen meanders several kilometres long snake to the estuary, and the alluvial plain is frequently waterlogged (the Ivry-Creteil plain between Seine and Marne is a classic flood zone). Subsurface control is decisive: the basin's aquifers (notably the Cretaceous chalk) supply on average 67% of the surface flow of the Seine at Poses, the artificial upstream limit of the estuary, which is why the regime is steady for a river of this size (PIREN-Seine, 2024). Climate and regime: temperate oceanic, with the 'degrade' continental nuance upstream; regime classed 'pluvial oceanique'; high waters December-April (February peak, over 600 m3/s at Paris), low flows from July (under 100 m3/s in a dry summer; reservoir releases guarantee at least 70 m3/s) - mean flow 310 m3/s at the Austerlitz gauge and 485 m3/s at Poses. Downstream: the Seine becomes a tidal estuary - the maritime reach from Rouen is about 120 km, tide propagates past Rouen, the famous mascaret tidal bore once ran far inland, and only four bridges cross it below Le Havre area (Normandie, Tancarville, Brotonne and the lifting Gustave-Flaubert at Rouen), all with 50 m clearance, so ferries carry the road traffic. Geomorphological note: the Paris channel is not natural - Holocene alluvial drift pushed the river south, and from the 18th century it was progressively embanked, with the bed lowered and straightened for navigation.
area_km2: [uncertain] Catchment (basin versant) of the Seine: 78,600 km2 according to DRIEAT Ile-de-France ('Evaluation preliminaire des risques d'inondation 2024', which also gives a 776 km course); scientific literature gives 76,238 km2 at the mouth (Lestel, Meybeck et al.); the Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie publishes 75,000 km2; French Wikipedia and popular sources give 79,000 km2. The [uncertain] flag is set because authoritative sources differ by up to about 5%, depending on whether the estuary and small Normandy inflows are counted and on the delineation used (Sandre WFD boundaries vs. topographic divide). Not to be confused with the much larger administrative river-basin district (Seine-Normandie): 94,500 km2, about 18-19% of metropolitan France, including the coastal rivers of Normandy. A river has no land area of its own; for comparison, the city it bisects covers 105.40 km2 (Paris).
river_length_km: [uncertain] Total length: 774.76 km in the Sandre national hydrographic reference (fiche cours d'eau 'La Seine', code ----0010; the Sandre page itself rounds this to 775 km). Other official figures: 776 km (DRIEAT Ile-de-France, EPRI 2024), 777 km (Ville de Paris and most institutional communication; GIP Seine-Aval; Initiatives-Rivers), 773 km (Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie), 782 km (Orange, Etudes normandes, 2015), 781 km (Britannica). All agree on about 775-777 km; the [uncertain] flag marks a 4-8 km spread across authoritative sources (measurement of an estuarine river's source-to-mouth axis). Length within Paris: 13 km intra-muros (Ville de Paris, 'La Seine, coeur battant de Paris'), the figure used by all official Paris communication; a 2007 regional study measured 14 km within the city and 24 km for the whole engineered 'bief de Paris' (24.990 km between Port-a-l'Anglais and Suresnes, VNF). Structure of the length: about 607 km of river proper plus about 170 km of fluvial and saline estuary (Lestel/Meybeck); navigable over 517 km from Marcilly-sur-Seine with 25 locks (some sources give about 560 km from Méry-sur-Seine); 450-540 km of the basin's waterways are large-dimension gauge.
river_source: [uncertain] Location (not in doubt): the spring of the Seine rises in the commune of Source-Seine, departement de la Cote-d'Or, region Bourgogne-Franche-Comte, on the Langres Plateau about 30 km north-west of Dijon, at 47 deg 29' 10" N, 4 deg 43' 01" E, on the watershed line between the Channel and Mediterranean drainage basins. Elevation (uncertain): 446 m is the figure used by French Wikipedia, derived from the IGN geodetic levelling marker Z.C.R3-7 (exactly 446.765 m in the IGN69 normal-height system, with the marker itself 0.75 m above the ground); the Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie gives 450 m, the Initiatives-Rivers synopsis 452 m, the Seine-en-Partage association 471 m and tourist sources 470 m - hence the [uncertain] flag on the elevation only. Details: the spring emerges from a spring cave exploited since Gallo-Roman times; Napoleon III's 1864 visit led to a grotto and a nymph statue by Jouffroy (erected 1865) donated to the Empress Eugenie; the sources and their surroundings have been the property of the City of Paris since 1864 (Wikipedia) / 1865 (GRIDAUH legal study prepared for the City), which is why the capital owns the head of its river; the site is a protected natural monument and public garden in the commune of Source-Seine (the commune was called Saint-Germain-Source-Seine until the late 1960s; the similarly named 'Sources-de-Seine' is a neighbouring commune created in 2016, a frequent source of confusion).
river_mouth: The Seine discharges into the English Channel (French: la Manche) through the Bay of the Seine, its mouth lying between Le Havre (Seine-Maritime) on the right (north) bank and Honfleur (Calvados) on the left (south) bank, at 49 deg 26' 02" N, 0 deg 12' 24" E, at an altitude of 0 m. The mouth is a funnel-shaped, macrotidal estuary - GIP Seine-Aval treats the stretch from the sea upstream to Le Vaudreuil / the Poses dam (roughly 170 km, about 120 km of it the 'maritime' reach from Rouen) as one estuarine system; the Poses barrage is the artificial upstream limit of tidal propagation, and the estuary receives about 435-534 m3/s mean freshwater inflow from upstream plus inputs from its banks and the chalk aquifer. The embouchure supports France's largest port system: HAROPA PORT (Le Havre, Rouen and Paris, merged 1 June 2021), with Le Havre (founded 1517) the leading French container port (3.1 million TEU in 2024) and Rouen a major grain terminal; the maritime reach is dredged continuously to 10 m draught for ships up to 280 m and 150,000 dwt. Crossings are few (Pont de Normandie, Tancarville, Brotonne, lifting Gustave-Flaubert at Rouen) with ferries completing the road network.
departments_crossed: [uncertain] Per the Sandre-based inventory of riverside communes, the Seine's own course touches 14 departements (its basin extends over 28 departments in 6 regions). Upstream to downstream: (1) Cote-d'Or (21) - source, Châteauneuf-sur-Seine, Châtillon-sur-Seine, Sainte-Colombe-sur-Seine, Vix; (2) Aube (10); (3) Marne (51) - a short reach at Marcilly-sur-Seine, Conflans-sur-Seine, Esclavolles-Lurey, where the Aube also joins; (4) Aube again (10) at Troyes/Rosieres; (5) Seine-et-Marne (77) - Bray-sur-Seine, Nogent-sur-Seine (boundary), Montereau-Fault-Yonne, Melun, Davron/Conflans-Sainte-Honorine boundary; (6) Essonne (91) - left bank from Corbeil-Essonnes to Evry-Courcouronnes (with Seine-et-Marne on the right); (7) Val-de-Marne (94) - Marne confluence, Charenton-le-Pont (right), Ivry-sur-Seine and Alfortville (left); (8) Paris (75); (9) Hauts-de-Seine (92) - Boulogne-Billancourt, Issy-les-Moulineaux, Suresnes, Saint-Cloud, Sèvres, Rueil-Malmaison, Nanterre, Gennevilliers, Asnières; (10) Seine-Saint-Denis (93) - a short left-bank reach at Saint-Denis and L'Ile-Saint-Denis; (11) Val-d'Oise (95) - right bank from Bezons/Argenteuil and Cormeilles-en-Parisis, La Frette-sur-Seine, Herblay-sur-Seine, Vétheuil, Haute-Isle, La Roche-Guyon - the Epte, which joins here, forming the Val-d'Oise/Eure limit (the historic Normandy border); (12) Yvelines (78) - left bank from Poissy, Les Mureaux, Mantes-la-Jolie, Bonnières-sur-Seine; then, downstream of Conflans-Sainte-Honore, both banks at various points, and later the left bank opposite Eure; (13) Eure (27) - right bank from Les Andelys, Louviers, Pont-de-l'Arche, Elbeuf (the Seine forms the Eure/Yvelines and then the Eure/Seine-Maritime departmental boundary); (14) Seine-Maritime (76) - both banks, Duclair, Grand-Couronne, Rouen, Le Grand-Quevilly, Lillebonne, Le Havre; and finally Calvados (14), skirted only at the extreme end of the estuary mouth on the Honfleur side. Caveats behind the [uncertain] flag: the count varies by source (French Wikipedia's infobox lists 12, its own body text and Sandre 14; the Seine-en-Partage association lists 13 and leaves out Calvados), and some hiking/summary lists wrongly include Yonne (89) or Nievre (58) - the Seine never flows through either, only its affluents do (the Yonne joins at Montereau, and its reservoir lake Panneciere is in the Nievre); the exact ordering of the short interlaced boundary reaches (92 / 93 / 95 / 78) is reconstructed from the Sandre commune list.
major_tributaries: Banks are given looking downstream; 47 tributaries feed the Seine. Right bank: the Ource (100 km, 736 km2, at Merrey-sur-Arce/Bar-sur-Seine); the Aube (248.9 km, 4,660 km2, 41 m3/s, at Marcilly-sur-Seine - the biggest upstream contributor, so much so that the Seine upstream of the junction has the smaller basin 4,000 km2 / 33 m3/s); the Voulzie (at Longueville-le-Chatelet area); the Yerres (98 km, 1,030 km2, at Villeneuve-Saint-Georges); the Marne (514.3 km, 12,920 km2, 110 m3/s, at Charenton-le-Pont / Alfortville / Ivry-sur-Seine - the last affluent before Paris and the watergate to Champagne); the Oise (341.1 km, 16,667 km2, 110 m3/s, at Conflans-Sainte-Honore/Andresy - largest tributary basin, rising in Belgium); the Epte (112.5 km, 1,490 km2, at Giverny/Limetz-Villez, where it also forms the Normandy regional limit); and the Andelle (57 km, at Pitres). Left bank: the Yonne (292.3 km, 10,836 km2, 93 m3/s, at Montereau-Fault-Yonne); the Loing (142.7 km, 4,150 km2, at Saint-Mammes/Moret-Loing-et-Orvanne); the Essonne (101.1 km, 1,870 km2, at Corbeil-Essonnes); the Orge (54 km, at Athis-Mons/Choisy); the Bièvre (the small stream that shaped the Latin Quarter, culverted in the 19th century and partly daylighted since); the Mauldre and Vaucouleurs (Yvelines); the Eure (228.7 km, 6,017 km2, 26.2 m3/s, at Saint-Pierre-les-Elbeuf / Pont-de-l'Arche); and the Risle (144.7 km, 2,300 km2, joining the estuary at Berville-sur-Mer/Saint-Samson-de-la-Roque). Three affluents are formally the 'majeurs' for the water agency: Yonne, Marne and Oise, with the Aube and Loing significant upstream of the Paris region and the Eure and Risle in Normandy. Hydrological caveat, well documented: at Montereau the Yonne carries more water (93 m3/s) and a larger basin (10,836 km2) than the Seine (80-93 m3/s, 10,300 km2), so a strict application of the naming rule (the downstream name follows the branch with the greater mean flow) would make the river flowing through Paris the Yonne, and the 'real' Seine a sub-tributary of the Yonne via the Aube; the traditional name prevailed for historical reasons, and the Yonne's source is also higher (738 m in the Morvan vs 446-450 m).
population_value: [uncertain] A river has no population; the applicable figures for the Seine are, depending on definition: (i) the Seine watershed proper gathers about 30% of the population of France (DRIEAT / AESN), commonly given as about 17 million (Initiatives-Rivers, 'a basin in which 17 million people live'); (ii) the whole administrative Seine-Normandie river-basin district counts 18.9 million inhabitants in 2022, 28% of the French population, of whom about 65% (some 12 million) live in Ile-de-France, which occupies only 13% of the district's area, and about 2 million live along the lower Seine valley or the nearby coast (Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie, Etat des lieux 2025); (iii) the conurbation the river crosses is Ile-de-France with 12,463,067 inhabitants (1 Jan 2023, INSEE), whose central city Paris - which the Seine divides - holds 2,103,778 (2023), with 11,013,774 in the Paris urban unit. The [uncertain] flag reflects the choice between watershed (about 17 M / 30%), administrative district (18.9 M / 28%) and served agglomeration (12.5 M).
population_date: Reference figures: INSEE (Institut national de la statistique et des economiques), populations municipales de reference at 1 January 2023, authentified by decree n° 2025-1362 of 26 December 2025, in force from 1 January 2026, published December 2025 (Paris 2,103,778; Ile-de-France 12,463,067). Basin population: Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie, Etat des lieux 2025 (basin population 18.9 M for 2022), adopted by the basin committee on 9 December 2025. Economic data used: INSEE regional accounts, 2024 result (provisional), published 10 November 2026. River statistics: VNF 2025 traffic year, published April 2026. Research performed 27-28 November 2026.
population_density: [uncertain] For the river basin: the Seine-Normandie district averages about 190-200 inhabitants per km2 (DRIEAT Ile-de-France EPRI 2024 gives about 190 hab./km2, 'almost double the national average'; 18.9 M inhabitants over 94,500 km2 gives 200 hab./km2) - and the population is heavily concentrated along the water: density rises from upstream towards the Paris region and again along the lower Seine to Rouen and Le Havre, while interfluves upstream of Paris fall below 20 hab./km2. For the city the Seine crosses: Paris 19,959.9 hab./km2 (INSEE 2023: 2,103,778 inhabitants over 105.40 km2, the most densely populated department of France) and Ile-de-France 1,038 hab./km2, against 107.6 hab./km2 for France as a whole. The [uncertain] flag is set because a density figure for a river is only meaningful for the basin or district served, not the watercourse.
capital_designation_history: (Field concerns the capital, Paris; recorded here as the Seine-side context.) 508: Clovis makes Paris his capital after Tournai and Soissons, residing probably at the palace of the Baths (Thermes) on the Left Bank and dying there in 511; despite frequent Merovingian partitions Paris keeps an undivided symbolic status as seat of the kingdom. Carolingian centuries: power is itinerant and oriented east (Aachen); Paris is abandoned, then fortified against the Viking raids from 845 (Charles the Bald repairs the wall of the Cite and fortifies its only bridge). 987: the election of Hugh Capet, descendant of Robert the Strong count of Paris, brings the dynasty back - under Philip I and above all Philip II Augustus (1180-1223) Paris becomes the effective capital: the Louvre is built, the royal archives are installed permanently at the Palais de la Cite, the Curia regis (later the Parlement de Paris), then the Chambre des comptes and the Cour des aides, are sedentarised there; by 1297 the city holds about 200,000 people, making it the largest in medieval Europe. 15th-16th centuries: the royal chancery itself calls Paris 'capitale de la France' although the court is itinerant (Bourges and the Touraine chateaux during the Hundred Years War; a rival new-capital project at Romorantin in 1516 is abandoned); Francis I fixes his residence in Paris from 1528, and from Henry III the Louvre becomes the main royal dwelling. 1682: on 6 May Louis XIV moves the court and the seat of government to Versailles, which remains the centre of the kingdom until 1789 without Paris losing its title of capital (the king continues to build colonnades and royal squares in Paris). 1789: the women's march of 5-6 October forces the royal family back to the Tuileries and the Constituent Assembly follows - the political-capital status of Paris is reaffirmed and has never lapsed since; the First Republic is proclaimed on 21 September 1792 and Louis XVI executed on the Place de la Revolution (now Concorde) near the Seine. 19th century: provisional seats in no way removed capital status - Tours and Bordeaux in 1870-71 during the Franco-Prussian war, and Versailles as the seat of the National Assembly from March 1871 (the Chamber sat in the chateau's opera house, then the new Salle du Congres from 1876) until the deputies returned to the Palais-Bourbon in 1879, while presidents had already begun residing at the Elysee from 1874. 20th century: Bordeaux again briefly in September 1914 and June 1940, and Vichy 1940-44 as the seat of the 'French State'; after the Liberation of Paris on 25 August 1944 de Gaulle's provisional government restored Paris as the seat of the constitutional powers. Fifth Republic (1958): the Constitution does not say it - the placement of both chambers in Paris rests on Article 1 of the ordinance of 17 November 1958, which also allows the seat of public authorities to be moved to another town, an act that would not in law change the capital. In short: capital by royal decision (508), by administrative sedimentation (12th-13th centuries), by convention and ordinary law (since 1958), never by constitutional text.
historical_role_of_river: Trade and provisioning: from the Merovingian period the Seine and its affluents were the principal commercial arteries feeding Paris - firewood and charcoal floated in drives from the Morvan down the Yonne (and, once the Ourcq was canalised around 1560, to Paris directly), Burgundy and Champagne wine, Brie and Beauce grain, Picardy timber, building stone from the Paris Basin quarries, iron, later coal, oil and construction materials; specialised unloading berths line both banks in the Middle Ages (the right bank held about two-thirds of them because the north channel was deeper): wine ports at Bercy and the quai Saint-Bernard/Jussieu, firewood and charcoal at Saint-Paul and Louviers, timber above the Bastille creek - which is how the Faubourg Saint-Antoine became the cabinet-makers' quarter. The Seine also powered the city (mills hung from bridges and moored to banks, washer-women's boats, bathing establishments) and supplied its water, pumped famously from under the Pont de la Samaritaine, before the springs of the Avre and the Dhuis/Vanne canals took over in the 19th century. Defence and urban form: Lutetia was born on the Ile de la Cite; the river served as moat and obstacle (the Viking sieges of 845-885 forced the fortification of the Cite and its single bridge), split the city into Cite (episcopal and royal) on the island, Ville (universities, Left Bank) and University quarter, and Faubourg Saint-Germain, and Haussmann's north-south boulevards were articulated on its crossings; the Seine also determined the port of the Greve (today's place de l'Hotel-de-Ville), the main medieval landing place, unquayed deliberately until the late 18th century so boats could touch ground at any water level. Institutions and city government: the river created Paris's municipality - the Hanse of the Merchants of the Water obtained royal charters (Louis VI 1121; Louis VII 1170) granting them the monopoly and police of navigation on the Seine from the Grand Pont to Mantes, extended by 1300 from the Pont de l'Arche to Corbeil (and over the Yonne to Sens, the Marne to Meaux, the Oise to Compiegne), the right to compel out-of-town merchants to 'hanser' and partner a Parisian bourgeois, and monopolies on unloading, gauging and criage of wine and grain; from this grew the Prevot des marchands with four aldermen, who became the head of the municipality under Louis IX and, at their apogee under Etienne Marcel, a political actor - their ship remains on the arms of Paris. The guild also imposed 50 m towpaths on each bank, the clearing of obstructions and the upkeep of bridges and ports. Naming of departments: the Revolution's law of 22 December 1789 / creation of 4 March 1790 named four departments after the river - la Seine (whose prefecture was Paris), Seine-et-Marne, Seine-et-Oise and Seine-Inférieure; Seine-Inférieure was renamed Seine-Maritime on 18 January 1955 (so a Parisian prefect could be 'prefect of the Seine' until the law of 10 July 1964 broke up the department of the Seine and Seine-et-Oise, effective 1 January 1968, into Paris (75), Hauts-de-Seine (92), Seine-Saint-Denis (93) and Val-de-Marne (94) on the one hand and Yvelines (78), Essonne (91), Val-d'Oise (95) on the other) - the river's name is thus inscribed in the map of the capital region. Industry, exhibitions and leisure: 19th-century canalisation (Charles Poiree's hinged gated dams, 1838) fixed a 3 m navigation depth in Paris and fed the industrial quays and the ports of Bercy, Ivry and Gennevilliers; the banks hosted the universal exhibitions of 1855, 1867, 1878, 1889 (Eiffel Tower) and 1900 (Grand Palais, Pont Alexandre III, esplanade des Invalides), pleasure cruising began in 1867 and the Bateaux-Mouches date from 1949; and the river remains today both the region's ecological corridor and, after a 1.4 billion euro clean-up, a swimmable urban waterway - a complete reversal of its 1960s-1980s state, when only a couple of fish species survived in the Paris reach (34-36 species today).
government_institutions_located: Not applicable to the river as such - the Seine is not a commune or territorial collectivity and hosts no seat of government. Seine-side facts: all the national institutions of the capital stand in Paris, mostly within a few hundred metres to about a kilometre of the river and several directly on its banks or on the island it washes - the Assemblée nationale at the Palais-Bourbon, whose facade fronts the Left Bank quay; the Senate at the Palais du Luxembourg (about 1 km from the Left Bank, the Congress meeting in the Salle du Congres at Versailles); the Presidency of the Republic at the Elysee and the Prime Minister at Matignon, both close to the Right/Left Bank embankments; the Conseil constitutionnel (Palais-Royal, 1st arr., a few hundred metres from the Right Bank); the Cour de cassation on the Ile de la Cite, bounded by the quays de l'Horloge and Bethune on the Seine, with the historic law courts (Conciergerie, Sainte-Chapelle) on the same island; the Grand Chancery of the Legion of Honour and the Musée d'Orsay on the Left Bank quay; and the ministries in charge of the river itself - ecological transition/transport, overseas and the sea - on Left Bank sites near the quai d'Orsay and avenue du Maine. On the water the State is present through Voies navigables de France, HAROPA PORT, the EPTB Seine Grands Lacs, the DRIEAT and Vigicrues flood-forecast services, the Prefecture of Police river brigade (maitres-nageurs and patrol boats) and the Paris fire brigade's river unit.
administrative_divisions: River-management districts and subdivisions of the Seine. (1) Basin scale: one of France's six hydrographic districts, Seine-Normandie (Sandre district code F), governed by the basin committee and the Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie, whose 94,500 km2 territory is divided for management into five sub-basins: the Seine from source to the Oise confluence, the Seine from the Oise confluence to its mouth, the Marne, the Oise and the Normandy coastal rivers; the district covers 28 departments, 6-8 regions and 8,000-8,700 communes and is planning under the EU WFD/Flood Directives via the SDAGE and the EPRI/PAPI programmes. (2) Waterway scale: VNF's territorial direction 'Bassin de la Seine et Loire aval' manages 1,400 km of navigable water (800 km of rivers, 600 km of canals) in 5 regions and 18 departments, of which about 450-540 km large-dimension, through 6 route units (UTI), 57 navigation dams, 253 locks and 16 navigation canals; below Rouen the estuary and ports belong to HAROPA PORT, created on 1 June 2021 by merging the autonomous ports of Le Havre, Rouen and Paris and today running 6 multimodal platforms (Gennevilliers, Bonneuil-sur-Marne, Limay, Bruyeres-sur-Oise, Evry, Montereau) and about 70 urban ports plus more than 40 passenger calls in Ile-de-France, of which over 20 inside the bief de Paris; the City of Paris operates the Paris canals. (3) Technical reaches of the river: Petite Seine (source - Montereau), Haute Seine (Montereau - Paris), Seine parisienne (in Paris), Basse Seine (Paris - Rouen) and Seine maritime (Rouen - sea) for navigators; and for engineering purposes the pooled 'bief de Paris', 24.990 km between the Port-a-l'Anglais (and Saint-Maurice) and Suresnes dams, normal pool 26.72 m, plus upstream biefs such as those of Suresnes and Meulan. (4) Basin-authority partnerships: the EPTB Seine Grands Lacs (four reservoir lakes and 3,000 ha of forest), other EPTBs along the course and its affluents, the 'Entente Axe Seine' grouping Paris, Rouen, Le Havre and the Metropole du Grand Paris, and the interministerial delegation for the Seine valley. (5) Local government along the river in the capital region: 170 riverine communes in Ile-de-France within 8 departments (Paris 75, Hauts-de-Seine 92, Seine-Saint-Denis 93, Val-de-Marne 94, Val-d'Oise 95, Yvelines 78, Essonne 91, Seine-et-Marne 77) and public territorial establishments (Etablissement public territorial, etc.). (6) Historical division: the departement de la Seine (1790-1967), replaced around the Paris reach by the four departments listed above.
economic_significance: Regional weight: the region the Seine bisects, Ile-de-France, produced a GDP of 866 billion euros in 2024 (provisional), i.e. 30.2% of metropolitan France's GDP (2,863 billion euros) - and in 2023 some 29.9-31.2% depending on the base used - making it the EU's richest NUTS-2 region (797 billion euros in purchasing-power standards, just ahead of Nordrhein-Westfalen and above Belgium or Ireland), with GDP per inhabitant 87% above the provincial average and 190% of the EU average (INSEE, 10 Nov 2026; Region Ile-de-France). Functions concentrated on the river: headquarters of large groups and extended producer services (business services 21.8% of regional value added), information-communication (58% of metropolitan VA in the branch) and financial services (54%) - La Defense, the Seine-frontage business district; wholesale, transport and warehousing 17.9% of VA; the concentrated State (22% of metropolitan non-market services VA). Port and inland-waterway role: the Seine is France's foremost inland axis and the corridor to France's first port group, HAROPA PORT (Le Havre-Rouen-Paris, over 102 Mt/yr of maritime and fluvial traffic in 2024, about 160,000 jobs, first French container port at 3.1 million TEU in 2024, first grain port of western Europe, first French river port, and - by its own account - the world's first port for river tourism). River freight: the Seine basin moved 16.56 million tonnes in 2025 (2,965 million t-km, equal to about 825,000 lorries avoided and 200,000 t of CO2 saved), i.e. 38% of France's river tonnage and 51% of tonne-kilometres (VNF, 22 April 2026); the record was 23.7 Mt in 2019 and the long-standing share of national traffic is 40-50%. Mix: construction materials 57% (9.55 Mt), agriculture 20%, plus metal, chemicals/fertilisers and containers (262,000 TEU on the Seine in 2025 after a 2024 record; more than 220,000 TEU moved between Le Havre and the Seine axis). Paris-specific flows: about 4 Mt/yr of goods still moved within Paris intra-muros (2017); urban river logistics reached 134,000 t in 2025 (+14%) over some 1,400 voyages (+120% vs 2021), including IKEA (Limay), La Poste/Fludis barges to Boulogne and Bercy, SYCTOM waste and earthmoving spoil from the Grand Paris Express (5 Mt moved by water to end-2025); Gennevilliers is the region's first multimodal platform (401 ha, 250 firms, 8,000 direct jobs, 380,000 TEU capacity). Capacity and investment: convoys up to 5,000 t below Paris, 3,000 t upstream and on the Oise; the reach is not saturated and could absorb 3-4 times today's traffic; the 107 km Canal Seine-Nord Europe (target service 2031-2032, objective cost about 7.3 billion euros, 4,400-t barges) plus Seine/Oise/Lys upgrades complete the trans-European Seine-Escaut link (TEN-T North Sea-Mediterranean corridor), and a 'chatiere' lock will give river craft direct access to Le Havre's Port 2000. Other economic functions: power-station cooling water, industrial abstraction, irrigation, low-flow support releases (which keep navigation and water quality possible in droughts), small hydroelectricity, and river tourism (see tourism_and_landmarks).
cultural_heritage_sites: UNESCO World Heritage: 'Paris, Banks of the Seine' (site no. 600) was inscribed in 1991 by the 15th session of the Committee under cultural criteria (i), (ii) and (iv) - a river landscape uniting masterpieces from the Middle Ages to the 20th century (Notre-Dame, the Sainte-Chapelle, the Louvre, the Pont Neuf, the Mint, the Invalides, the Ecole militaire, the Grand and Petit Palais, the Pont Alexandre III, the Palais de Chaillot, the Eiffel Tower) and the town-planning layers of the capital of one of Europe's first great nation-states; the property comprises the bridges, quays and banks of the historic course between the Pont de Sully and the Pont d'Iena (extended to the Pont de Bir-Hakeim on the Left Bank) together with the Ile de la Cite and the Ile Saint-Louis in their entirety, 365 ha and 23 of the 37 Paris bridges. A retrospective Statement of Outstanding Universal Value was adopted in 2017, and a minor boundary modification (file 600bis, ICOMOS report approved 13 March 2024, inscribed 2024) extended the site upstream to the Austerlitz viaduct, downstream on both banks to the Pont de Bir-Hakeim, included the Ile aux Cygnes and all buildings facing the river, bringing the area to 531 ha; the property still has no buffer zone, and UNESCO flags urban development, traffic pollution and tourism pressure on its visual and urban integrity. The protection rests on French law as well: the classified/registered monuments, the 'site patrimonial remarquable' of Paris, and the public-river-domain status of the banks and quays. Related heritage on the lower Seine: the rebuilt centre of Le Havre at the mouth (Auguste Perret) is itself on the World Heritage list; the estuary and the meanders downstream of Paris carry Natura 2000 protection and the Regional Natural Park of the Boucles de la Seine normande; the Sources of the Seine (the 1865 grotto and nymph monument, property of the City of Paris) are a protected and visited natural monument; and the river's engineering heritage - the 19th-century Poiree gated dams and locks, the Paris 'murettes' and quay walls, the movable bridges of the estuary (Brotonne, Gustave-Flaubert) - is separately inventoried and protected.
tourism_and_landmarks: The river is itself a top attraction: VNF and HAROPA rank the Seine as the fourth most visited 'monument' of Paris, ahead of the Eiffel Tower. Excursion boats ('bateaux-mouches' and 58 companies with some 130 vessels) carried about 8.5 million passengers in Paris in 2025 (+8% on 2024), part of 10.5 million nationally of which 84% in Ile-de-France; the Seine basin concentrates about 80% of French river-tourism traffic, with 174 boats active in the region (VNF/E2F, April 2026). HAROPA counts more than 9.5 million passengers a year, a network of over 40 river calls in Ile-de-France (20+ inside the bief de Paris) berthing 55 boats simultaneously and about 6,000 ad hoc calls a year. Cabin cruising is growing fast: cruise calls on the Seine axis +15.8% in 2025 - Paris 464, Rouen 982, Vernon 730 - with the fleet of river cruise ships rising from 21 (2024) to 23 (2025), 26 in 2026 and 31 planned for 2027, and occupancy near 90%. Landmarks on or facing the water, with 2025 attendances: Notre-Dame on the Ile de la Cite, more than 11 million visitors in the twelve months after its 7 December 2024 reopening (free entry; the towers, reopened in September 2025, took 110,017 climbers); the Louvre, 9.0 million (right bank); Sainte-Chapelle, 1,333,286 (Centre des monuments nationaux, whose network reached a record 12 million in 2025); the Eiffel Tower on the Champ de Mars (left bank), 6.75 million paying levels (+7%) and about 10 million on the free esplanade; Musee d'Orsay, Invalides, Grand Palais, Trocadero/Chaillot, Place de la Concorde, Bibliotheque Francois-Mitterrand ( reached by the Passerelle Simone-de-Beauvoir, the 37th crossing), Paris Plages and the Rives de Seine, the La Defense frontage, and, downstream, Rouen's quays and the estuary's four great bridges; the Route des Impressionnistes (Auvers-sur-Oise to Le Havre) markets the valley. New uses: three supervised free swimming sites opened in the capital in July 2025 (Bras Marie below the Ile Saint-Louis, Bras de Grenelle in the 15th, Bercy in the 12th), first public swimming in the Seine for about a century, after the Olympic and Paralympic open-water triathlon events held in the river in July-August 2024.
flood_risk_management: Notable floods. The reference event is the 'crue centennale' of January 1910: the water rose in about ten days, peaked at 8.62 m on the Austerlitz gauge in Paris on 28 January 1910 (a discharge of 2,400 m3/s in the official Paris PPRI table, up to 2,650 m3/s in some reconstructions) and stayed above normal for some 45 days, flooding most of the valley and central Paris (deputies travelled to the Assemblée nationale by boat; the Zouave of the Pont de l'Alma had water to his shoulders). It is the largest recorded flood since that of 1658. Benchmarks on the same gauge: 1924 7.30-7.32 m; 1945 6.85 m; 1955 7.12-7.14 m; 1970 5.63 m; 1982 6.16-6.18 m; 2001 5.21 m; and June 2016, when the Seine reached 6.10 m at Austerlitz around 02:00 on 3-4 June 2016 (1,750 m3/s), its highest level for 34 years - 15,000 people evacuated and about 1 billion euros of damage across the Loire and Seine basins, the Louvre, Orsay, Grand Palais and two BnF sites closed and works moved to higher ground, the RER C and metro stations shut, with the reservoir lakes almost full and therefore shaving only about 5 cm off the Paris peak (25 cm during the recession). The May-June 2016 event also exposed an instrument failure: the only Paris gauge (Austerlitz) under-reported the level by some 30 cm for hours because debris blinded its sensors. Current system of protection. (a) Upstream regulation by four 'lacs-reservoirs' run by the EPTB Seine Grands Lacs: Panneciere on the Yonne (80 Mm3, 1949), lac de la Seine/Forest of Orient (208 Mm3, 1966), Der-Chantecoq on the Marne (350 Mm3, 1974, Europe's largest such reservoir) and Amance-Temple on the Aube (170 Mm3, 1990) - about 800-850 Mm3 in total, plus a transferable 17 Mm3 on the Cure chain (Crescent, Chaumecon, operated with EDF); flood control runs 1 November to 30 June, low-flow support 1 July to 31 October. Their limits are explicit: they regulate only about 17% of the catchment above Paris, act with about an eight-day lag, and their 0.8 billion m3 compares with the 3-5 billion m3 that passed Paris above the 3.20 m alert level in 1910; modelled benefit for a 1910-type flood is a lowering of about 70 cm at Paris (1.0-1.2 m together with local works and in-channel improvements). (b) In and around the capital: quay walls and 'murettes' protecting to the 1910 level (8.60 m), bridges raised and the channel deepened at the downstream exit of Paris since 1910, mobile flood barriers, pump-station management, the SIAAP wastewater works and, in May 2024, the Austerlitz stormwater/storage basin (about 50,000 m3, twenty Olympic pools) that cuts sewage overflows during heavy rain. (c) Planning and warning: the 1910 water levels are the reference hazard for the flood-risk plans (PPRI) of Paris and every upstream/downstream department (Paris PPRI report adopted 15 July 2003, alert level 3.20 m at Austerlitz); the City is notified daily by the Prefecture of Police from 2.50 m, RATP protective works are triggered at 6.60 m; forecasts and warnings come from Vigicrues and DRIEAT's 'Seine Moyenne Yonne Loing' forecast service (Vigicrues colour codes and the Paris flood plan, with boat-based warning of houseboats). The Ile-de-France 'Strategie inondation francilienne', approved in December 2023, plans on a reference scenario of 115% of the 1910 discharges (9.1 m at Austerlitz), noting that for exactly the 1910 discharge today's water level would be about 8.12 m because of works since; it stresses that existing works are designed for 10-30-year events and would be overtopped by a major flood. (d) Planned measures: the 'Seine-Bassee' flood-expansion casier in Seine-et-Marne and the Longueil-Annel extension on the Oise, both carried by EPTBs, together with protected flood-expansion zones in the middle Marne valley and the Bassee plain, plus continuing relocation of assets in the floodplain, flood-awareness education and the PAPI Seine et Marne franciliennes 2023-2029 programme. (e) Residual risk is a live policy issue: the insurance and economic modelling of a 1910-type flood today would stop metro and RER lines, underground car parks, the tourist river fleet and riverside utilities, and the 2024 Olympic works were explicitly justified partly by this double flood/water-quality exposure.

confidence_level: High for the core question and for the structural facts: that the Seine is the river running through Paris (the capital of France), its source at Source-Seine (Cote-d'Or), its mouth between Le Havre and Honfleur, the 13 km Paris reach with 37 bridges and its two islands, the arrangement of banks and arrondissements, the UNESCO 'Paris, Banks of the Seine' inscription of 1991 (extended 2024), the 1910 reference flood of 8.62 m at Austerlitz and the current flood-protection system, and the absence of any constitutional or statutory definition of the French capital (confirmed directly on Legifrance, in the Council of Europe study and in a 2024 peer-reviewed law article). All of these were verified against state or official bodies: Sandre/OFB, DRIEAT Ile-de-France, VNF, HAROPA PORT, the Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie, Vigicrues/PIREN-Seine, INSEE, UNESCO and the Ville de Paris. Medium for several single-value physical and demographic statistics, where the official sources themselves disagree and I have had to publish a range: total length (773-781 km), catchment area (75,000-79,000 km2), source elevation (446-471 m), the number of departments the river itself crosses (12-14) and the population 'of the river' (about 17 M for the watershed vs 18.9 M for the administrative district vs 12.5 M for Ile-de-France). Medium-low on the most recent 2025-2026 figures (INSEE 2024 GDP is provisional; Notre-Dame's 11 million visitors is a free-entry twelve-month estimate; tourism counts use non-comparable methods) and on the ordering of the short inter-departmental boundary reaches, which I reconstructed from the Sandre commune list rather than reading it directly.
